project.title: Where a Tree Gets Its Carbon

cues.text: Look at a tree outside your window. Its trunk feels solid, heavy, and very different from the air around it. Where did that material come from? A common first answer is the soil. Roots do take up water and minerals, but the carbon in a tree's organic molecules comes mainly from carbon dioxide in the air. Photosynthesis is the process that brings that carbon into the living world.

We need to separate two questions: where the atoms come from, and where the energy comes from. Carbon dioxide and water provide atoms. Light supplies energy. Light is not an ingredient that turns into carbon atoms. During photosynthesis, the plant uses energy to rearrange matter into molecules that can store chemical energy. Keeping matter and energy separate makes the whole process much easier to understand.

A leaf brings together the ingredients and structures needed for photosynthesis. Tiny pores, called stomata, allow carbon dioxide to enter. Water arrives through the plant's transport tissues. Inside leaf cells, chloroplasts contain the machinery that captures light and builds organic molecules. A leaf is not simply a green solar panel. It is also a place where gases move, water travels, and many connected chemical reactions take place.

Why do many leaves look green? Chlorophyll absorbs some wavelengths of light more strongly than others, especially in the red and blue regions. A greater proportion of green light is reflected or transmitted, so green is the color that often reaches our eyes. Saying that plants are green because they absorb only green light reverses the explanation. Leaf color is a clue about which light is not absorbed as strongly.

None of this means that soil is unimportant. Plants need minerals, water, and a suitable environment for their roots. Those resources support growth, but they play different roles from carbon dioxide. When we say that much of a plant's dry organic material comes from the air, we are following carbon atoms. We are not saying that a plant can live without roots, water, or mineral nutrients.
